messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Nowak is a 45-year-old widowed military medic of Polish descent who presented for an initial psychological evaluation following a referral from his unit's medical officer. He carries a PCL-5 score of 66, placing him firmly in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a man who has survived something that fundamentally unmade him.

Eighteen months ago, Aleksander was deployed as part of a humanitarian relief operation in the aftermath of a catastrophic earthquake in a mountainous region overseas. He had worked disaster zones before, and he arrived with the practiced competence of a man who had spent two decades keeping others alive under pressure. What he encountered in the first seventy-two hours overwhelmed every framework he had brought with him. The earth had moved without warning in the early morning hours, and the village his team was tasked with clearing had partially collapsed inward — buildings folded on top of families still in their beds. Aleksander worked continuously through the rubble, triaging survivors and recovering the dead, often guided by sound: a child's cry from beneath a concrete slab, the groan of a man pinned under timber, and then, more frequently as the hours passed, silence where sound had been. At one point, a secondary tremor struck while he was inside a partially standing structure, and the sudden roar of shifting debris — a sound that he describes as the earth itself tearing — sent him flat to the ground over a casualty he could not save. He was not physically injured. He kept working. He did not stop for four days.

In the months that followed his return, Aleksander found that the world had been rearranged in ways he struggled to articulate. Unexpected sounds — a door slamming in the barracks corridor, a truck backfiring on the base road, the sudden clatter of equipment in the medical bay where he works — sent him into a state of rigid alertness that did not resolve quickly. He began scanning his environment with the focused attention of a man expecting collapse, even in rooms he knew to be structurally sound, even in moments that by every rational measure were safe. He could not let that vigilance go. At night, attempting to sleep, he remained coiled. The inability to relax was not a feeling he could talk himself out of; it was physical, constant, and exhausting.

When memories of the disaster returned, they did not come as coherent narrative. Aleksander described fragments — a face, a sound, a particular quality of dust in the air — that arrived without order and without context. He could not reconstruct a reliable sequence of events even when he tried deliberately, and this disorientation distressed him almost as much as the content itself. When he attempted to recall what happened, the terror he had suppressed during those four days returned with full force, and the emotional weight was so overwhelming that he had to stop, to put the memory down before it consumed him entirely. He had come to avoid any deliberate engagement with those days as a result, which had begun to affect his clinical documentation — reports filed late, details omitted, a growing reluctance to debrief with colleagues who had been there alongside him.

What frightened him most, he said quietly in their second session, was not the sounds or the memories but something harder to name. He had been a man who believed that skill and preparation could hold the worst at bay, that meaning could be found in the work of saving lives, that he understood who he was and what he stood for. He had buried his wife three years earlier and had rebuilt himself around purpose and service. Now he was certain that none of that had ever been real. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. He did not recognise himself in the mirror — not the face, but the person behind it. His beliefs about the world, about effort and agency and the value of what he did, felt like architecture that the earthquake had quietly destroyed.

He sought help, finally, because he had made a clinical error at work — minor, caught in time, but enough. He was most afraid that there was no version of himself left to recover.
